summary: Updates the round-trip time estimation used by TFRC-based congestion control in DCCP by adding a Sender RTT Estimate option. It updates the CCID-3 and CCID-4 specifications and addresses parameter-estimation problems that arise with TFRC-based DCCP congestion control.

eli5.summary: To send data at a good speed you need to know how long a message takes to go and come back. This gives senders a way to share their own measurement so the speed is chosen more accurately.

questions: what is the dccp rtt estimate option
what is dccp send rtt estimate feature
why does tfrc need sender rtt
subtitle: Lets a DCCP sender tell the receiver its own round-trip time measurement, instead of the receiver guessing it.

tldr.problem: In DCCP's TFRC-based congestion control (CCID-3 and CCID-4), the receiver estimates the round-trip time from a coarse 4-bit counter, which gives infrequent and inaccurate samples, especially during loss.
tldr.mechanism: A new RTT Estimate option (number 128) lets the sender report its own RTT measurement in microseconds, and a Send RTT Estimate feature (number 128) negotiates whether the sender must include it.
tldr.outcome: When the feature is on, the receiver uses the sender's value everywhere it needs an RTT. This RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4342 and RFC 5622.

today: RFC 6323 is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted by any later RFC. It updates RFC 4342 (CCID-3) and RFC 5622 (CCID-4).

sections.title: Why Move RTT Sampling to the Sender
sections.content:
The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP, RFC 4340) offers congestion-controlled but unreliable datagram delivery. Each congestion control method is named by a Congestion Control Identifier (CCID). CCID-3 (RFC 4342) and the experimental CCID-4 (RFC 5622) both follow TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC, RFC 5348), which paces packets over a round-trip time (RTT) rather than sending them back-to-back.

Because pacing and the computed sending rate depend directly on the RTT, an accurate estimate matters. The original CCID-3 and CCID-4 specifications have the receiver estimate the RTT using the cyclic 4-bit window counter in the DCCP CCVal header. Experience showed this gives infrequent and inaccurate measurements.

This document follows a recommendation from RFC 5348, Section 3.2.1: measure the RTT at the sender, which gives more reliable and more frequent samples. It updates both CCIDs.
sections.eli5: It is like timing a ball thrown back and forth. The thrower holding the stopwatch gets a better time than the catcher guessing from the side.

sections.title: Problems With Receiver-Side RTT Sampling
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes several years of experience with the Linux implementation of CCID-3 and CCID-4. The receiver-based algorithm of RFC 4342, Section 8.1 uses a coarse counter (units of RTT/4) and packet inter-arrival times. Four problems follow:

  • It only works for packets whose modulo-16 CCVal difference is less than 5, so other samples must be discarded.
  • Holes in the sequence space (from delay, reordering or loss) make counter wrap-around impossible to detect, so sampling pauses exactly when loss happens.
  • Inter-arrival times are a poor stand-in for network gaps. Network cards may deliver packets in bunches, so arrival gaps can converge to zero.
  • Under-sampling: if loss occurs before the receiver has a sample, it falls back to a fixed constant and the connection can slow down needlessly.

Heavy filtering of the samples did not substantially help. The sender, in contrast, has timestamps and elapsed-time information, which are mandatory in CCID-3.
sections.eli5: The receiver was trying to work out the trip time from a rough clock that keeps wrapping around, and it lost track whenever a message went missing. The sender has a much better clock for the job.

sections.title: What Else Depends on the RTT
sections.content:
A bad RTT estimate spreads to other parts of the receiver. The RFC lists six areas that depend on it: the measured receive rate X_recv, the synthetic first loss interval, separating loss events, validating loss intervals, making sure at least one feedback packet is sent per RTT, and detecting quiescence.

An explicit RTT lets the receiver measure X_recv more accurately and isolates failures. It lets the receiver separate loss events more reliably, because a loss event is defined as losses within one RTT. The quiescence period is defined as max(2 * RTT, 0.2 sec), so a good RTT avoids under- or over-estimating it.

The RFC also notes simpler implementations, fewer unnecessary expirations of the nofeedback timer, and that middleboxes can use the option to verify that a flow uses conforming end-to-end congestion control.
sections.eli5: Lots of decisions use the trip time, like when to send a progress report. If that one number is wrong, all the decisions go a bit wrong, so fixing it helps everything.

sections.title: The RTT Estimate Option
sections.content:
The RTT Estimate option has option number 128 and may be placed in any DCCP packet. It comes in three valid formats, with total length 3, 4 or 5 bytes, carrying a value of 1 to 3 bytes. Multi-byte fields are in network byte order.

The value is the sender's current RTT estimate with a granularity of 1 microsecond, which allows values up to 16.7 seconds (0xFFFFFE). A sender that samples more finely SHOULD round up to the next microsecond. Special values:

  • 0 means no valid RTT sample yet; the sender MUST use it if it has no estimate.
  • Estimates under 1 microsecond MUST be reported as 1 microsecond.
  • 0xFFFFFF is reserved to signal a delay spike larger than 16.7 seconds, a qualitative warning that something is wrong, such as jamming on a wireless channel.

The sender SHOULD pick the smallest format that fits, without leading zero bytes.
sections.eli5: The sender writes its stopwatch reading on a small note, using as few digits as it can. A zero means it does not have a reading yet, and all nines means the trip is taking forever.

sections.title: The Send RTT Estimate Feature
sections.content:
Use of the option is governed by a DCCP feature, Send RTT Estimate, with feature number 128. It is server-priority, takes a 1-byte Boolean value (values above 1 are reserved) and has an initial value of 0, so it is off by default.

The feature is OPTIONAL: not every DCCP implementation has to understand it. To require the other side to send RTT Estimate options, DCCP B sends a Mandatory Change R(Send RTT Estimate, 1). If DCCP A does not understand the feature, it resets the connection.
sections.eli5: Both sides have to agree before the sender starts writing the notes. It starts switched off, and one side can ask for it to be switched on.

sections.title: Using the Option and Receiver Safeguards
sections.content:
When the feature is enabled, the sender MUST put an RTT Estimate option on all Data, DataAck, Sync and SyncAck packets, and MAY add it to others such as DCCP-Ack. If the RTT exceeds 0xFFFFFE, it sends 0xFFFFFF. The sender must still maintain the CCVal window counter.

The receiver MUST use the reported value in every place that needs an RTT. If it sees an invalid option, it MUST reset the connection with Reset Code 5, "Option Error". When the feature is off, the old receiver-based estimation applies.

The receiver SHOULD keep a long-term estimate, called receiver_RTT, using a moving average. Safeguards in Section 3.4:

  • Until the first numeric option arrives, receiver_RTT MUST be 0.5 seconds, to match the initial 2-second nofeedback timeout. A previously known path RTT MAY seed it instead.
  • During occasional no-number options (0 or 0xFFFFFF), the receiver SHOULD keep its long-term value.
  • If no-number options last longer than receiver_RTT, the receiver MUST set receiver_RTT = MIN(2 * receiver_RTT, t_mbi), where t_mbi is 64 seconds.
  • The receiver MAY close the connection when receiver_RTT reaches MAX_RTT.
sections.eli5: If the notes stop having real numbers, the receiver does not panic. It keeps its old guess for a while, then slowly assumes the trip is longer and longer, and may finally give up.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Altering the RTT Estimate value could interfere with a TFRC flow. Since RTT accuracy affects the measured sending rate X_recv, an attacker could cause higher or lower sending rates than network conditions warrant. This requires being on the path between sender and receiver and guessing valid sequence numbers, so the considerations in RFC 4340, Section 18 apply.

IANA is asked for identical allocations in the dccp-ccid3-parameters and dccp-ccid4-parameters registries: option 128 for RTT Estimate and feature number 128 for Send RTT Estimate, both in the CCID-specific range 128..191.
sections.eli5: Someone sitting in the middle who could change the number might trick the sender into going too fast or too slow. They would also need to guess some hard-to-guess counters, which makes it difficult.
